pages.name: Breaking capacity
pages.task: A protective device sits where the prospective fault current is 3 kA. What must its breaking capacity be?
pages.answer: At least 3 kA, the most it may have to break there
pages.why: Breaking capacity is the biggest current a device can safely interrupt. A fault just past it can draw the prospective fault current, 3 kA here. So the device must break at least 3 kA. Its rated current and the cable's rating are about everyday load, far smaller.

pages.name: A short at the terminals
pages.text: A real 12 V block holds six cells in one case. Each cell is an emf behind a small resistance. Together they read 12.6 V open circuit, with 6.95 mΩ inside. Short the terminals, and that resistance alone holds the current back. So the [[short-circuit current]] is the open-circuit voltage ÷ the internal resistance. Here that is 12.6 ÷ 0.00695 = 1813 A. The maker lists 1814 A for this block. That is far above the device's 1 kA. With the fault across the terminals, 1813 A flows.

pages.name: A spanner across it
pages.task: You lay a steel spanner across the terminals of the same 12 V block. What flows?
pages.answer: Up to about 1800 A, held back only by the block's milliohms and the spanner
pages.why: The spanner joins the terminals with almost no resistance. So the block's own 6.95 mΩ is nearly all that holds the current back. 12.6 ÷ 0.00695 is about 1800 A. A low voltage only means a small current through a high resistance, like your body. That current makes the spanner very hot very quickly. It can explode in a shower of molten metal, which burns and can light hydrogen.

pages.name: Down the cable
pages.text: With the fault further down the cable, both cores join the loop, out and back. So the current is the voltage ÷ (the battery's resistance + the outside resistance). The battery's milliohms are fixed. Only the loop outside can add more. Each core has 0.5 mΩ a metre, so each metre adds 1 mΩ. At 5 m the loop is 6.95 + 5 = 11.95 mΩ. So 12.6 ÷ 0.01195 = 1054 A flows, still above the device's 1 kA.

pages.name: Ten metres down
pages.task: A fault happens 10 m down the same cable. What is the fault current?
pages.why: Ten metres of route puts both cores in the loop, out and back. At 0.5 mΩ a metre each, they add 10 mΩ. The loop is 6.95 + 10 = 16.95 mΩ. So the current is 12.6 ÷ 0.01695 = 743 A. That is now below the device's 1 kA.

pages.name: A big string
pages.text: The same rule works for a real 480 V string. The cells' resistance and the links between them set the most a battery can drive. This string's loop adds up to 0.160 + 0.028 Ω. So the rule predicts 480 ÷ 0.188 = 2553 A, about 2550 A. A real test on that string measured 2530 A. A shorted battery can give 100 to 1000 times its normal discharge current. Here the big string drives 2553 A.

pages.name: A 48 V string
pages.task: A 48 V string has 24 cells at 2.1 V, each with 1.5 mΩ inside. Its 23 links between cells add 0.1 mΩ each. These are example values. What flows in a fault across its terminals?
pages.why: One current flows through every cell, so the resistances add. The cells give 24 × 1.5 = 36 mΩ. The links add 23 × 0.1 = 2.3 mΩ. The open-circuit voltage is 24 × 2.1 = 50.4 V. So the current is 50.4 ÷ 0.0383 = 1316 A.

pages.name: Running down
pages.text: Let the charge fall from 100% to 60%, and the fault current barely moves. A cell's rested voltage falls only a little as its charge goes. The milliohms stay milliohms. In tests on real batteries, the current stayed above 90% of its full-charge value at about 60% charge. So a part-discharged battery can still give nearly its full fault. In this sketch, the block still drives 1668 A at 60% charge.

pages.name: Run down to 60%
pages.task: A UPS battery has run down to about 60% charge. Someone says a short on it now would be small. Are they right?
pages.answer: No: its fault current is still over 90% of the full-charge value
pages.why: The fault current is the voltage ÷ the loop resistance. As the charge falls, the rested voltage drops only a little. The milliohms stay milliohms. So the current hardly changes. In tests it stayed above 90% of its full-charge value at about 60% charge.

pages.name: At once, and always live
pages.text: The trace shows the current from the moment of the fault. A battery has little inductance, so a short acts like a fault through a plain resistor. The current reaches its full value within 5 to 10 ms. The cells cannot be switched off either. Their exposed metal is always live. Switching off the charger and the loads stops their currents. The cells keep their voltage.

pages.name: A loose link
pages.task: You must remake a loose link between two cells in a live string. What comes first?
pages.answer: Switch off the circuits on the battery, and keep metal tools off its top
pages.why: Switching off the circuits stops the charger's and the loads' currents. It does not make the cells dead. Their exposed metal is always live. So keep tools off the top, where a spanner could bridge two terminals. Use insulated tools, and work on one connection at a time.

pages.name: Other chemistries
pages.text: Other chemistries obey the same fault rule, but their cells differ. Lithium-ion brings a new hazard, [[thermal runaway]]. A cell's own heat speeds its reactions, and they make more heat. The card sets all three side by side.

pages.name: Nickel-cadmium charge
pages.task: A nickel-cadmium battery needs its charge checked, and a hydrometer is to hand. What will the hydrometer tell you?
pages.answer: Nothing about the charge, because the electrolyte is not used up in the reaction
pages.why: In a lead-acid cell, the acid takes part in the reaction. Discharge uses it up, so the liquid thins and the float sinks. A nickel-cadmium cell's potassium hydroxide only carries the current. Its strength stays the same at any charge. So the float reads the same, full or part charged.

pages.name: Can it clear it?
pages.task: A 24 V emergency battery has 12 lead-acid cells at 2.1 V and 14 mΩ in total, links included. A fault 2 m down its cable adds 2 mΩ. The device there can break 1 kA. These are example values. Can the device clear the fault?
pages.why: Twelve cells at 2.1 V give 25.2 V. The loop is the battery's 14 mΩ plus the cable's 2 mΩ, which makes 16 mΩ. So the current is 25.2 ÷ 0.016 = 1575 A. A device that breaks only 1 kA cannot clear it safely.

pages.name: A lithium-ion pack
pages.task: A pack of 3.60 V lithium-ion cells is to replace that 24 V lead-acid battery. How many cells in series does it need, and can a hydrometer check its charge?
pages.why: Each lithium-ion cell gives 3.60 V. Six would fall short of 24 V, so it takes 7, which make 25.2 V. Its cells are sealed, so there is no liquid to draw off. A hydrometer has nothing to read.
